data.title: Morphea (localised scleroderma) — viva
data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Morphea (localised scleroderma)** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define morphoea.**
- Localised scleroderma — inflammatory sclerosing disease of the skin and underlying tissues (fat, fascia, muscle, bone) without Raynaud's, sclerodactyly or internal organ involvement; does not progress to systemic sclerosis

**Q2. Classify morphoea (Padua / Laxer–Zulian classification).**
- Circumscribed (plaque) — superficial or deep (morphoea profunda)
- Linear — trunk/limbs, or head (en coup de sabre, progressive hemifacial atrophy/Parry–Romberg)
- Generalised — ≥4 plaques >3 cm in ≥2 of 7 anatomical sites; includes isomorphic/symmetric types
- Pansclerotic — circumferential involvement of limbs including bone, children, risk of SCC in ulcers
- Mixed (e.g. linear + circumscribed)
- Others: guttate, keloidal/nodular, bullous, atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini, eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman) — related

**Q3. Clinical features of plaque morphoea.**
- Oval indurated plaques with ivory-white shiny centre and a violaceous/lilac border (active inflammation — 'lilac ring'); later hyper- or hypopigmented atrophic patches with loss of hair and sweating
- Trunk (bra-line, waist), proximal limbs

**Q4. Linear morphoea — why important in children?**
- Commonest type in children; along a limb, may cross joints → contractures, limb-length discrepancy, muscle atrophy, growth failure
- En coup de sabre (frontoparietal 'sword-cut' depression of scalp/forehead with scarring alopecia) — may have neurological (seizures, headache) and ocular involvement
- Needs early systemic therapy (methotrexate) and physiotherapy

**Q5. Pathogenesis.**
- Unknown: endothelial injury and inflammation (Th1/Th17 early, Th2 later) → TGF-β-driven fibroblast activation and collagen deposition
- Triggers: trauma (Koebner), radiation (post-radiation morphoea of breast), infections (Borrelia burgdorferi in Europe — debated), drugs, vaccinations; autoimmune association (ANA, anti-ssDNA, anti-histone in linear/generalised)

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Clinical diagnosis; biopsy (deep incisional) if doubt
- ANA, anti-ssDNA, anti-histone (correlate with deep/active linear disease), eosinophilia (in eosinophilic fasciitis), CBC
- MRI (deep tissue/brain in en coup de sabre), ultrasound and thermography for activity; LoSCAT (localised scleroderma cutaneous assessment tool — mLoSSI activity and LoSDI damage)

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Early (inflammatory): perivascular and interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at dermal–subcutaneous junction, swollen collagen
- Late (sclerotic): thick hyalinised collagen bundles parallel to the surface throughout dermis, loss of adnexa (trapped eccrine glands without surrounding fat), square 'punch biopsy' sign, reduced CD34 dendritic cells

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Systemic sclerosis (Raynaud's, sclerodactyly), lichen sclerosus (overlap), post-inflammatory pigmentation, vitiligo, scleredema, lipoatrophy (steroid injection), necrobiosis lipoidica, eosinophilic fasciitis (groove sign, peau d'orange, eosinophilia), radiation fibrosis, morphoeic BCC, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis

**Q9. Management.**
- Limited plaque disease: potent topical steroids, tacrolimus, calcipotriol (± betamethasone), imiquimod; intralesional steroid for active border
- Phototherapy: UVA1 (medium dose) or PUVA/bath PUVA for widespread plaques; NB-UVB for superficial
- Systemic (linear, generalised, pansclerotic, deep, functionally threatening, en coup de sabre): methotrexate 15 mg/m²/week (max 25 mg) + systemic corticosteroids (pulse IV methylprednisolone or oral) for 3 months, continue MTX ≥12–24 months; mycophenolate if MTX fails; tocilizumab, abatacept, JAK inhibitors for refractory
- Physiotherapy for contractures; surgical correction/fat grafting for atrophy once inactive

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Plaque morphoea usually softens over 3–5 years leaving pigmentation; linear and deep forms cause lasting deformity; relapse in ~25–30% (especially childhood linear)

**Q11. Describe generalised and pansclerotic morphoea.**
- Generalised: ≥4 indurated plaques >3 cm in ≥2 body sites (trunk, thighs) — may be isomorphic (bra/ waistband areas) or symmetrical; more systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthralgia), ANA positive
- Pansclerotic: disabling, circumferential involvement of limbs/ trunk including bone, sparing fingertips; children; non-healing ulcers with SCC risk; aggressive immunosuppression needed

**Q12. What is morphoea profunda (deep morphoea)?**
- Sclerosis of deep dermis, subcutis, fascia — bound-down, ill-defined induration with overlying normal or slightly pigmented skin ('cobblestone'/ groove), arms/legs/trunk; overlaps with eosinophilic fasciitis; treat systemically

**Q13. What is atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini?**
- Considered an abortive/ burnt-out superficial morphoea: well-defined slightly depressed grey-brown patches with 'cliff-drop' borders on the back of young adults, no induration; benign slow course; doxycycline/ hydroxychloroquine reported

**Q14. Extracutaneous involvement in morphoea.**
- Arthralgia/ arthritis, joint contractures, limb-length discrepancy, myalgia (linear/ deep types)
- Neurological (en coup de sabre/ PRS): seizures, headache, brain lesions on MRI
- Ocular: uveitis, episcleritis, eyelid atrophy — eye screening in children with head/face linear morphoea

**Q15. How do you assess disease activity?**
- Clinical: new lesions or extension, erythema/ violaceous border, warmth, induration progression (LoSCAT — mLoSSI for activity, LoSDI for damage)
- Imaging: infrared thermography (warmth — false positives in atrophic lesions), high-frequency ultrasound, MRI for deep disease; laser Doppler flowmetry

**Q16. Morphoea and lichen sclerosus overlap — significance.**
- Up to 5–10% of morphoea patients have extragenital LS, and genital LS coexists in some — examine genitals in all morphoea patients (genital LS needs specific treatment and has SCC risk)

## Quick spotter facts
- Ivory-white indurated plaque with lilac ring — morphoea
- En coup de sabre — linear morphoea on forehead
- Methotrexate + steroids for linear disease

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Morphoea); Padua consensus classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
